title: Nivolumab every 2 weeks for head and neck cancer
context_label: Recurrent or metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck after platinum treatment; the cancer cannot be treated with curative local therapy and has progressed or returned within six months of the last platinum dose.
indication_text: Recurrent or metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck after platinum treatment; the cancer cannot be treated with curative local therapy and has progressed or returned within six months of the last platinum dose.
purpose: Nivolumab aims to control head and neck cancer that has returned or spread, relieve symptoms and help some people live longer. Benefit and side effects are reviewed for you.
schedule_summary: Nivolumab is given as 240 mg through a vein over 30 minutes OR 600 mg as an injection under the skin over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 2 weeks. Your team selects one formulation; these doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Allow extra time for safety checks, preparation and observation. Treatment continues until the cancer progresses or side effects become unacceptable, with individual benefit and safety review. There is no fixed number of cycles in this head and neck treatment course.
administration_text: Nivolumab is given as 240 mg through a vein over 30 minutes OR 600 mg as an injection under the skin over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 2 weeks. Your team selects one formulation; these doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Allow extra time for safety checks, preparation and observation.
monitoring_summary: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests and glucose before every 2-week cycle. Thyroid tests once a month and when indicated; cortisol when clinically indicated.

agents.name: Nivolumab
agents.explanation: Nivolumab blocks PD-1 on immune cells, helping them recognise and attack cancer. It can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.
agents.watch: Report new breathing, bowel, skin, hormone, heart or nerve symptoms promptly; these may be immune inflammation.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, hormone glands, skin, heart and nervous system
Some effects need steroids, hospital care or long-term hormone replacement
Effects may start after the final dose

support.title: Immune alert card and treatment holds
support.text: Carry your immune alert card during and after nivolumab. Tell any clinician that you have received immunotherapy. Do not restart a held treatment or change prescribed steroids or hormone replacement yourself.

support.title: Eating and weight
support.text: Tell the team early if swallowing, appetite, pain or taste changes reduce intake. A dietitian can agree practical food, drink or feeding support with you. Do not wait for substantial weight loss.

support.title: Mouth and dental care
support.text: Agree a mouth-care plan and tell your dentist about previous or current cancer treatment. Arrange oncology advice before dental procedures, particularly after head and neck radiation.

support.title: Swallowing and communication
support.text: Ask for speech and language therapy if swallowing or speech is difficult. Use the food textures, exercises and communication support advised for you; a general guide cannot establish safe swallowing.

support.title: Medicines and fertility
support.text: Bring prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines and supplements for review. Discuss fertility preservation and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least five months after the final dose. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Do not breastfeed without specific advice from the team.

chapters.title: Your diagnosis and treatment aim

items.title: The setting for this guide
items.text: Recurrent or metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck after platinum treatment; the cancer cannot be treated with curative local therapy and has progressed or returned within six months of the last platinum dose.

items.title: What treatment aims to do
items.text: Nivolumab aims to control head and neck cancer that has returned or spread, relieve symptoms and help some people live longer. Benefit and side effects are reviewed for you.

items.title: Choosing between treatments
items.text: Your team weighs the cancer, previous treatment, health, symptoms and preferences when discussing options. Other systemic treatment, local treatment where suitable, trials or symptom-focused care may be discussed.

chapters.title: How your treatment works
chapters.intro: Cancer treatment can also affect healthy tissue.

items.title: Nivolumab
items.text: Nivolumab blocks PD-1 on immune cells, helping them recognise and attack cancer. It can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.

chapters.title: Your treatment schedule
chapters.intro: Keep one calendar for treatment, tests and other appointments.

items.title: Receiving treatment
items.text: Nivolumab is given as 240 mg through a vein over 30 minutes OR 600 mg as an injection under the skin over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 2 weeks. Your team selects one formulation; these doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Allow extra time for safety checks, preparation and observation.

items.title: Length of the course
items.text: Treatment continues until the cancer progresses or side effects become unacceptable, with individual benefit and safety review. There is no fixed number of cycles in this head and neck treatment course.

items.title: A pause or change
items.text: Your team may pause or stop treatment to assess side effects. Record the reason, required tests and who can authorise restarting. A new cycle does not erase earlier severe toxicity.

items.title: Changing nivolumab schedule
items.text: When switching from two-week to four-week dosing, the first four-week dose is given two weeks after the last two-week dose. In the reverse direction, the first two-week dose is given four weeks after the last four-week dose. Your team confirms the actual switch date and formulation.

chapters.title: Tests and review
chapters.intro: Blood safety tests, tumour tests and scans answer different questions.

items.title: Before the first dose
items.text: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and thyroid tests; review autoimmune disease, transplants, previous immune side effects and all medicines.

items.title: During the course
items.text: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests and glucose before every 2-week cycle. Thyroid tests once a month and when indicated; cortisol when clinically indicated.

items.title: Response assessment
items.text: Your team uses examinations, symptoms and scans in your individual cancer-assessment plan; ask when the next assessment is due and who will explain the result.

items.title: After treatment
items.text: Keep reporting new symptoms after treatment ends. Immune side effects require monitoring for at least five months after the last dose. Steroid tapers, hormone replacement or specialist review may continue longer. Scans and examinations follow your individual response and follow-up plan.

chapters.intro: Use the anatomical map with these explanations; location does not tell you how urgent a symptom is.

items.text: Severe headache, confusion, weakness, dizziness or marked thirst need prompt advice.

items.title: Lungs

items.title: Heart
items.text: Chest pain, racing heartbeat or fainting needs urgent assessment.

items.title: Liver

items.title: Kidneys

items.title: Bowel
items.text: New or persistent diarrhoea, blood in stools or severe tummy pain needs urgent advice.

items.title: Skin
items.text: Report a spreading rash, painful skin, blisters or peeling promptly.

items.title: Muscles / nerves

items.title: Eyes / vision
items.text: New blurred vision, painful eyes or visual change needs prompt advice.

chapters.title: When and how to get help
chapters.intro: Use the oncology service’s written urgent-contact plan.

items.title: Contact the team promptly
items.text: Contact oncology immediately for new breathlessness, chest pain, diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin or eyes, much less urine, severe headache, vision changes, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or a spreading or blistering rash. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or seizure is an emergency.

items.title: During an infusion or injection
items.text: Tell staff immediately about itching, a rash, dizziness, chest tightness, breathing difficulty, pain or swelling around the treatment site.

items.title: Prepare the handover
items.text: Tell the clinician the medicine name, date of the last dose, new symptoms and any prescribed steroids or hormone replacement. Carry the wallet card; do not delay urgent care while looking for a document.

chapters.title: Eating, mouth care and everyday support
chapters.intro: Ask for help before a practical problem prevents treatment.

items.title: Immune alert card and treatment holds
items.text: Carry your immune alert card during and after nivolumab. Tell any clinician that you have received immunotherapy. Do not restart a held treatment or change prescribed steroids or hormone replacement yourself.

items.title: Eating and weight
items.text: Tell the team early if swallowing, appetite, pain or taste changes reduce intake. A dietitian can agree practical food, drink or feeding support with you. Do not wait for substantial weight loss.

items.title: Mouth and dental care
items.text: Agree a mouth-care plan and tell your dentist about previous or current cancer treatment. Arrange oncology advice before dental procedures, particularly after head and neck radiation.

items.title: Swallowing and communication
items.text: Ask for individual speech and language therapy advice for swallowing or communication difficulties. Report choking, coughing with drinks or inability to swallow safely.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Plan manageable activity and rest around symptoms. Tell the team about severe or unexpected fatigue, falls or difficulties managing at home.

chapters.title: Medicines, precautions and visit preparation
chapters.intro: Review medicines and practical needs before treatment.

items.title: Medicines and fertility
items.text: Bring prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines and supplements for review. Discuss fertility preservation and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least five months after the final dose. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Do not breastfeed without specific advice from the team.

items.title: Access and observation
items.text: Intravenous treatment needs suitable venous access. Under-the-skin nivolumab is given into the thigh or abdomen, rotating sites and avoiding damaged skin, scars and moles. It is not given into a vein. Tell staff about local pain or swelling.

items.title: Work, transport and communication
items.text: Discuss transport, work, caring responsibilities, interpreter needs and a support person. Ask how results and changes will be communicated and who books your next tests.

chapters.title: Your record and contact card
chapters.intro: Keep the information that another clinician would need.

items.title: Cycle or review record
items.text: Record the cycle received, date, route, dose if supplied, important symptoms, any hold and the next agreed review. Stamp boxes record treatment received; they do not authorise the next dose.

items.title: Contacts and documents
items.text: Have the team replace example telephone numbers with your actual daytime and out-of-hours contacts. Carry the front/back wallet card and immune alert card when applicable. The printed handbook contains the key information without needing to scan a QR code.

items.title: Questions for review
items.text: Bring your main question, changes in swallowing or weight, symptoms, medicine changes and any concerns about the treatment aim. Ask for the plan in words you can explain back.

chapters.title: Evidence and further information
chapters.intro: Use evidence to support a personal treatment discussion.

items.title: What studies can tell us
items.text: CheckMate 141 found longer overall survival with nivolumab than the selected single-agent alternatives after platinum failure. The trial used weight-based intravenous nivolumab every two weeks. It did not separately randomise the current fixed-dose, four-week or under-the-skin schedules.

items.title: Your individual decision
items.text: Group results cannot predict what will happen for you. Ask which benefits matter for your situation and how the team will decide whether treatment remains worthwhile.

items.title: Resources
items.text: The source list gives the official regimen and public patient information. Ask your team for a printed copy or help accessing a resource if needed.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: Nivolumab aims to control head and neck cancer that has returned or spread, relieve symptoms and help some people live longer. Benefit and side effects are reviewed for you.
evidence.population: Recurrent or metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck after platinum treatment; the cancer cannot be treated with curative local therapy and has progressed or returned within six months of the last platinum dose.
evidence.comparison: Nivolumab versus investigator-selected methotrexate, docetaxel or cetuximab after platinum failure.
evidence.interpretation: CheckMate 141 found longer overall survival with nivolumab than the selected single-agent alternatives after platinum failure. The trial used weight-based intravenous nivolumab every two weeks. It did not separately randomise the current fixed-dose, four-week or under-the-skin schedules.
limitations: Trial results describe groups; your individual benefit and risks may differ.
Do not transfer survival estimates between different cancer settings, schedules or treatment combinations.

consent_support: Discuss your diagnosis, intent, alternatives, expected benefit and uncertainty, treatment burden, serious or lasting harms, fertility and pregnancy precautions and your priorities. Include immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, skin, glands, heart, muscles, nerves and eyes; infusion or injection reactions; delayed effects; possible high-dose steroid treatment, permanent hormone replacement or permanent treatment stopping. Confirm actual urgent contacts and use teach-back. This draft does not authorise treatment.
